Tankless water heaters heat water only when a tap opens, so there is no storage tank to keep hot and no 40- or 50-gallon limit on a long shower. This collection brings together every complete tankless unit we carry, gas, propane and electric, from Navien, Rheem, Noritz, Stiebel Eltron, Intellihot and IBC. Valve kits, vent pipe and repair parts are listed separately.

Gas, propane or electric

Natural gas units deliver the most hot water for the fuel cost and run from 120,000 to 199,900 Btu/h for whole-house use. Propane models are built for LP and suit homes off the gas main, and many Navien and Rheem IKONIC units are field-convertible between the two fuels. Electric tankless heaters need no vent or gas line, but an 18 to 36 kW whole-house unit draws roughly 75 to 150 amps, so check your electrical panel first. Small point-of-use models serve a single sink.

Condensing or non-condensing

Condensing units reach 0.93 to 0.96 UEF by recovering heat from the exhaust, so they vent through PVC, CPVC or polypropylene and need a condensate drain with a neutralizer. Non-condensing units cost less up front but need stainless steel Category III venting. Outdoor models skip indoor venting altogether.

Sizing in GPM

Size a tankless heater by flow rate, not by gallons. Add up the gallons per minute (GPM) of the fixtures that run at the same time, then check each unit's flow at your winter temperature rise. A 199,900 Btu/h gas unit gives about 5 GPM at a 70°F rise, enough for two showers at once in most of the country. Colder groundwater means less flow from the same heater. Our guide on what size tankless water heater you need walks through the math.

Frequently asked questions

What size tankless water heater do I need?

Add up the GPM of the fixtures that run at the same time and compare it with each unit's flow at your winter temperature rise. A 199,900 Btu/h gas unit gives about 5 GPM at a 70°F rise.

Is there a 120V tankless water heater?

Small point-of-use units such as the Rheem RTEH3512 run on 120V and serve one sink. Whole-house electric units need 240V. See point-of-use water heaters.

Can a tankless water heater use my old water heater vent?

No. Condensing units vent in PVC, CPVC or polypropylene, and non-condensing units need stainless Category III venting. Neither vents into an existing atmospheric flue.

A tankless heater has no storage, so it is sized by flow at a given temperature rise, not by gallons. The same unit that delivers 6 gpm in Texas delivers barely 3.5 gpm in Minnesota, because incoming groundwater is 30°F colder and the burner has a fixed maximum output. Size from your local winter inlet temperature and the fixtures that must run at once — two showers and a dishwasher is a different unit than one bathroom.

Condensing versus non-condensing decides the installation, not just the fuel bill. A 90%+ condensing unit extracts enough heat to condense flue gas, so it vents in PVC or polypropylene and needs a condensate drain with neutralization, since the condensate is acidic. Non-condensing units need stainless category III venting. Neither vents into an existing atmospheric flue.

Gas line sizing is the constraint that stops most retrofits: a 199,000 Btu/h unit typically needs 3/4" and often a meter upgrade. Check supply before ordering.

What size gas tankless water heater do I need?

Condensing or non-condensing?

Condensing units (90%+ efficient) vent in PVC, CPVC or polypropylene and need a condensate drain with a neutralizer. Non-condensing units need stainless steel Category III venting. Neither can use an existing atmospheric flue.

Can I switch between natural gas and propane?

Some models are field-convertible with the manufacturer's kit, and others are sold as separate natural gas and propane versions. Check the fuel type in the product title before ordering.

Navien tankless water heaters heat water on demand, with no storage tank to keep hot. This page lists every complete Navien unit we stock: the NPE-2 condensing series from the NPE-150S2 to the NPE-240S2 and NPE-240A2, rated up to 0.96 UEF, plus the mid-efficiency NHW700 and NPN lines. All are gas-fired, from 120,000 to 199,900 Btu/h. Choose the series first (condensing or not), then size by flow at your winter temperature rise. Every unit ships from Seattle, WA. Comparing brands? See Rheem tankless water heaters or all tankless water heaters.

16 Navien gas tankless units in three series, from the $1,005 NPN-160U at 160,000 Btu/h to the $2,910 NPE-240A2 at 199,900 Btu/h. Every unit takes 3/4" on cold inlet, hot outlet and gas, runs on 120V AC, and carries a stainless steel heat exchanger. Water pressure range is 15 to 150 PSI across the line.

The NPE-2 series is the condensing line and the reason to specify Navien. It runs 0.93 to 0.96 UEF on a dual stainless heat exchanger, primary and secondary, and vents through 2" or 3" PVC, CPVC or polypropylene at 0" clearance to combustibles. That clearance figure is what lets the unit go in a tight closet or a finished utility room where a hot-vented heater cannot. The NPE-2 is also rated to 10,100 feet, is certified to SCAQMD 1146.2 at under 20 ppm NOx, and every model except the NPE-150S2 is Energy Star certified.

Read the model number, not the suffix, for capacity. Navien numbers the NPE by nominal size, not by input: NPE-150S2 is 120,000 Btu/h, NPE-180 is 150,000, NPE-210 is 180,000 and NPE-240 is 199,900. Flow at a 67°F rise runs 3.4 GPM on the 150 up to 5.8 GPM on the 240S2.

S2 or A2 decides whether you buy a pump. The S2 is the base condensing unit and carries the higher efficiency number, 0.96 UEF. The A2 is ComfortFlow: a built-in recirculation pump and buffer tank inside the same cabinet, 0.95 UEF, and a minimum draw that drops to under 0.01 GPM instead of 0.5. On a retrofit the A2 removes the cost of an external pump, a crossover valve and the labor to mount them, which usually beats the $292 to $585 cabinet premium.

NHW700 and NPN are the mid-efficiency line. Both run 0.81 UEF on a single stainless exchanger and are Ultra Low NOx, and both are considerably lighter and smaller than the NPE: 55 to 65 lbs and 14" wide against 68 to 77 lbs and 17.3" wide. The NHW-SU and the NPN-U install indoors or outdoors, the NPN-E is exterior only, and the NHW700 AI models carry the same built-in pump and buffer tank as the A2.

Two things to confirm before ordering. The 3/4" gas inlet is the fitting size, not the supply sizing: a 199,900 Btu/h unit on an undersized or long gas run will fault under full demand, so size the pipe to the load. And on the NPE, the 0" vent clearance applies to approved vent material only, so budget the PVC or polypropylene run with the heater rather than after it.

Navien venting kits, recirculation components, isolation valve kits and repair parts are stocked separately.

Need heat as well as hot water? A Navien combi boiler does both from one wall-hung unit. See all Navien boilers.

Shop by model: NPE-240S2, NPE-240A2, NPE-210S2, NPE-210A2, NPE-180S2, NPE-180A2 and NPE-150S2. Compare them in the Navien model comparison.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between the NPE-240S2 and the NPE-240A2?

Both are 199,900 Btu/h condensing units. The NPE-240S2 is the standard model at 0.96 UEF. The NPE-240A2 adds ComfortFlow, a built-in recirculation pump and buffer tank, at 0.95 UEF.

What size is each Navien NPE model?

The model number is a nominal size, not the input. NPE-150S2 is 120,000 Btu/h, NPE-180 is 150,000, NPE-210 is 180,000 and NPE-240 is 199,900 Btu/h.

Can a Navien NPE run on propane?

Yes. The NPE-2 models listed here are NG/LP convertible. The NPN-U models on this page are sold as propane versions.

What venting does a Navien NPE need?

NPE-2 units vent through 2" or 3" PVC, CPVC or polypropylene and need a condensate drain. Use the venting and maximum lengths in the installation manual for your model.

Rheem tankless units across four series, from the 18 kW electric RTEX to the 199,900 Btu/h IKONIC with a built-in recirculation pump. Gas models run 120,000 to 199,900 Btu/h and deliver 3.3 to 5.6 GPM at a 70°F rise. Every gas unit takes 3/4" MIP on water and gas, holds 85 to 140°F, and modulates down to 11,000 Btu/h.

The choice that decides the install cost is condensing or not. The RTG series is non-condensing: 0.81 to 0.82 UEF, a copper fin heat exchanger, and exhaust hot enough to require 3"/5" stainless concentric venting. The RTGH series condenses: 0.93 UEF, copper and stainless, and exhaust cool enough to vent through 2" or 3" PVC, CPVC or polypropylene. The condensing unit often costs more on the invoice and less on the wall, because the vent material is a fraction of the price. Run both numbers before you pick.

IKONIC is the top tier. The RTGH-S models carry a full stainless heat exchanger, 0.96 UEF, a 15-year exchanger warranty instead of 12, and an elevation rating of 10,200 feet against 8,400 for the rest. The SR variants add a factory recirculation pump, which removes the cost of a separate pump and crossover valve on a retrofit.

Outdoor models need no vent at all. The XL suffix is outdoor, DV is indoor direct vent. In a mild climate the outdoor unit deletes the entire venting line item.

Two things to check before ordering. Size the gas supply to the load, not to the connection: the 3/4" inlet is the fitting, and a 199,000 Btu/h unit on an undersized run will fault under demand. And on electric, read the amperage before the kilowatts: the RTEX-36 draws 150 A and wants four 40 A breakers, which most residential panels cannot give up.

Repair parts, vent kits, valve kits and recirculation components for these units are stocked separately.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between Rheem RTG and RTGH?

RTG units are non-condensing and need stainless concentric venting. RTGH units are condensing, rated 0.93 UEF, and vent through PVC, CPVC or polypropylene.

What do DV and XL mean in a Rheem model number?

DV is an indoor direct vent model. XL is an outdoor model that needs no vent pipe.

What replaces a Rheem RTGH-95DVLN-2?

The RTGH-95DVLN-3 lists the RTGH-95DVLN-2 and RTGH-95DVLN-1 as replaced models. Each product page shows a "Replaces" list where we have that data.

Which Rheem tankless has a built-in recirculation pump?

The IKONIC SR models, such as the RTGH-SR10I and RTGH-SR11I, include a factory recirculation pump.

15 Noritz tankless units across four series, 157,000 to 199,900 Btu/h, priced $2,115 to $2,668. Every model modulates down under 18,000 Btu/h, so a single hand wash does not fire the burner at full rate.

Condensing or not is the first decision, and it changes the vent line item. The NRC, NRCP, NRCR and EZ series all condense and vent through 2" or 3" Schedule 40 PVC or CPVC. The NR98 does not condense: the SV model needs 4" Category III stainless and the DVC needs Noritz 5"/3" concentric stainless. Category III pipe costs several times what PVC costs, so the cheaper heater is frequently the more expensive installation.

The NR98 is the only line here that exceeds 140°F. It sets from 100 to 180°F against 100 to 140°F on every condensing model, and it runs a commercial-grade copper exchanger with 25% thicker piping. If the application needs sanitizing temperature or a hard-water tolerance, that is the reason to give up the efficiency.

The EZ series is built for retrofit. Noritz rates it for a 1/2" gas line, which is the single most expensive surprise in a tank-to-tankless conversion, since most existing tank installs have 1/2" run to the appliance. It carries a 316L stainless exchanger, 0.96 UEF and a 25-year residential heat exchanger warranty, against 12 years on the NRC line.

Recirculation is factory-fitted on two models. The NRCP111 and NRCP98 ship with the pump, and the NRCR92 carries Noritz recirculation as well. This matters beyond convenience: on the NRC line, adding an external recirculation loop to a model not built for it drops the heat exchanger warranty from 12 years to 3. Buy the recirculating model rather than adding a pump to a standard one.

Two things to check before ordering. Confirm the fuel: LP and NG are separate SKUs here, not a field conversion, except on the EZ111 Pro which is field convertible. And confirm the vent path before the unit, because on the NR98 the difference between SV and DVC decides which stainless system you are buying.

Heat pump water heaters move heat from the surrounding air into the tank instead of generating it, so they use a fraction of the electricity of a standard electric tank.

Rheem ProTerra hybrids run 40 to 80 gallons on a 240 V, 30 A circuit and keep 4,500 W elements as backup for high demand. The ProTerra 120 V plug-in models (40 and 50 gal) run from a standard outlet, which makes them the retrofit choice where a gas heater is being replaced and there is no 240 V circuit. The Sanco Gen5 is a split system: an outdoor CO2 heat pump paired with a separate storage tank.

Two things to plan for: the unit needs enough surrounding air volume to work (check the installation manual for the minimum room size or ducting option), and it produces condensate that needs a drain or a condensate pump. Set it in a drain pan where a leak would cause damage.

Popular in this collection: Rheem ProTerra 50 Gallon Hybrid PROPH50, Rheem ProTerra 65 Gallon Hybrid, Rheem ProTerra 80 Gallon Hybrid, Sanco Gen5 GS5-45HPC-D Outdoor Unit.

Frequently asked questions

Is a hybrid water heater the same as a heat pump water heater?

Yes. Hybrid is the common name for a heat pump water heater that also has electric elements. The heat pump does most of the work, and the elements back it up during high demand.

Do I need a 240V circuit for a heat pump water heater?

Most hybrid models, such as the Rheem ProTerra 40 to 80 gallon units, need a 240V circuit. The ProTerra 120V plug-in models run from a standard outlet, which helps when replacing a gas water heater without a 240V circuit.

Does a heat pump water heater need a drain?

Yes. The heat pump makes condensate, so the installation needs a condensate drain or a condensate pump, as well as the usual relief valve discharge. Check the installation manual for the air space the unit needs around it.

ProTerra 120V plug-in or 240V hybrid: which should I choose?

The ProTerra 120V plug-in (40 and 50 gallon) plugs into a standard 120V outlet, so it suits gas-to-electric replacements where there is no 240V circuit at the water heater. The 240V ProTerra hybrids (40 to 80 gallon) need a 240V, 30A circuit and add 4,500 W backup elements, which recover faster when demand is high. Where a 240V circuit is already in place, or the household uses a lot of hot water, the 240V hybrid is usually the better fit. Check the electrical requirements in the installation manual before ordering.

Every 40 gallon Rheem we stock, gas and electric, on one page: Professional Classic®, Professional Classic Plus® and Professional Prestige® residential tanks, light-duty commercial electric, and models listed for manufactured housing.

Gas or electric follows the house. Replace like for like unless you are prepared to run a new gas line or a 240 V circuit. Gas input on these runs from 30,000 to 50,000 Btu/h, and a higher input recovers faster after a long shower. The residential electrics are 240 V at 4.5 or 5.5 kW; the light-duty commercial electrics are 208 V at 6 kW.

On gas, venting is the real decision. Atmospheric models vent by natural draft into an existing B-vent or chimney. Powered damper (PD) models close the flue between cycles to cut standby loss. Power vent (PV) models use a blower to push exhaust through plastic pipe out a side wall, and power direct vent (PDV) models also bring combustion air in from outside. Match the vent to the house before comparing anything else.

On electric, height is the fit. The same 40 gallons comes in a medium height for a low ceiling or under a stair, and a tall, narrower tank for a tight closet. Measure the space, including clearance above for the connections.

Manufactured homes need a manufactured-housing model. The MH units here are listed for that use, including direct-vent versions that take combustion air from outside the closet.

Every 50 gallon Rheem we stock. That includes Professional Classic®, Classic Plus® and Prestige® residential tanks, high-input Prestige® Maximus gas models, ProTerra® hybrid and 120 V plug-in heat pump water heaters, and commercial units.

How to choose a 50 gallon water heater

Start with the fuel the house already has. Like for like avoids a new gas line or 240 V circuit.

On gas, match the venting. Atmospheric models use an existing B-vent or chimney. Powered damper models close the flue when idle. Power vent and power direct vent models use a blower and plastic pipe through a side wall. Higher input recovers faster.

On electric, check height and circuit. Residential models run on 240 V with 4.5 or 5.5 kW elements, in medium and tall heights. A heat pump model uses far less electricity but needs air space and a condensate drain.

Compare the first-hour rating on the spec sheet with your busiest hour of use. If 50 gallons is more than you need, see Rheem 40 gallon water heaters. Related: heat pump water heaters · tankless water heaters · water heater connectors · water heater pans · how to drain and flush a water heater

Commercial gas water heaters from 80,000 through 360,000 Btu/h, in atmospheric, power-vent and condensing configurations.

Commercial sizing works from first-hour rating rather than tank volume. The units here deliver from 264 to 419 gallons in the first hour, and that figure — storage plus recovery combined — is what determines whether a restaurant or a locker room runs out at peak. A large tank with slow recovery and a small tank with fast recovery can carry the same rating.

Efficiency splits the range roughly in half. Units at 90% and above are condensing: they extract enough heat to condense flue gas, which means PVC or stainless venting and a condensate drain with neutralization, since the condensate is acidic. Below 90% the appliance uses conventional metallic venting.

That difference decides the installation cost more than the appliance price does — a condensing replacement in a building plumbed for atmospheric venting means new vent, new drain and often a new gas line.

Connections are 1-1/2" and 2" MIP. Brands include Rheem and Noritz.

Commercial electric water heaters from Rheem, with maximum delivery temperatures of 170°F, 180°F and 181°F.

Commercial electric heaters run multiple elements on a staged contactor rather than one large element, which is what lets a single tank recover quickly without an impossible instantaneous draw. Recovery is a function of total kW and is the number to size from, alongside storage volume.

The temperature rating is the specification to check against the application. Commercial dishwashers require 180°F sanitizing rinse water, which is why 180°F-capable units exist as a distinct class — a heater topping out below that cannot serve the machine without a booster.

Anything delivering above 120°F to a fixture needs a thermostatic mixing valve downstream. Storing hot enough to control Legionella and delivering hot enough to scald are the same temperature; the mixing valve is what separates them.

Connections are 3/4" MIP and 1-1/2" NPT dielectric nipples — the dielectric fitting matters here, since the tank and the building piping are usually different metals.

Frequently asked questions

How do I size a commercial electric water heater?

Size from peak-hour hot water demand: storage volume covers the first draw, and recovery, set by total kW, covers the rest of the hour. Compare both numbers on the product page with the demand of the fixtures and equipment served.

Does the heater voltage have to match the building?

Yes. Order the heater for the voltage and phase available at the panel, such as 208V, 240V or 277V. Some models are field-convertible between voltages, which is listed on the product page.

What is a fused terminal block?

A fused terminal block adds fuses in the heater's wiring compartment, protecting the element circuits inside the heater. It is required on some larger commercial heaters; check the local electrical code and the installation manual.

This collection gathers Rheem-brand replacement parts listed under Rheem part numbers, many of them in the SP series, so you can match the number on the old part or in the unit's parts list.

Thermal expansion tanks for potable water systems, sized 0–5 gallons for residential and up to 60 gallons for larger installations, with mounting brackets.

These exist because of the check valve or backflow preventer on the incoming service. Once that device is fitted, the plumbing becomes a closed system: water heated in the tank expands and has nowhere to go, so pressure climbs until the T&P relief valve weeps. A weeping relief valve on a recently re-plumbed house is almost always this, not a faulty valve.

A potable tank is not a hydronic tank. It must be rated for drinking water, with a polymer-lined or stainless connection instead of the bare steel used on heating models, and it carries a different certification.

Pre-charge the tank to match your static water pressure before installing it, with no water in it. Charging afterwards reads the water side, not the air, and leaves a tank that is effectively full and doing nothing.

Connections run 1/2" through 1-1/4", MIP and FIP. Brands include Amtrol, Flexcon, Flamco and Zilmet.

Body HTML:
100 venting components for condensing gas appliances: polypropylene single wall (80), water heater vent kits (12), terminations and vent screens (7) and a concentric adapter, from Centrotherm, Noritz, Rheem, US Boiler, IPEX and DiversiTech. Vent pipe and fittings run 2" through 10".

A condensing appliance does not vent like an atmospheric one, and that is the whole reason this category exists. An 80% furnace or an atmospheric water heater sends hot, dry flue gas up a chimney or a B-vent on its own buoyancy. A 95% furnace, a condensing boiler or a tankless heater pulls most of that heat out first, so what leaves the appliance is cool, wet and acidic, and a fan pushes it. It will not rise, it will condense inside the vent pipe, and it will attack anything that is not built for it. That is why these systems are sealed, sloped and fan-rated rather than simply pointed upward.

The appliance manual decides the vent material, not the pipe aisle. Polypropylene systems are listed to UL 1738, the standard written for venting appliances with condensing flue gases — the listing is on the vent system as a system, gaskets and terminations included. PVC and CPVC are pressure-pipe standards; where they are used as vent it is because the appliance manufacturer's instructions permit it, not because the pipe carries a vent listing of its own. Either way the authority is the installation manual for the specific appliance, and mixing a listed system with unlisted parts voids the listing for the whole run.

Single wall or concentric is a penetration decision. Single wall runs exhaust and intake as two separate pipes, which is cheaper and more forgiving to route but needs two holes and a minimum separation at the terminations. A concentric vent carries intake around exhaust in one pipe, so the building gets one penetration and one termination that cannot be wrongly spaced — worth the extra cost through a finished wall, a roof, or anywhere the two terminations would otherwise be hard to place correctly.

Terminations are where inspections fail. Clearance to windows, doors, soffits, air intakes, gas meters and grade is set by code and by the appliance manual, and low-profile wall terminations exist precisely because those clearances are hard to hit on a tight lot. Bird and rodent screens belong on every outdoor opening; the ones stocked here cover 2" through 8".

Retrofit work usually means relining, not rebuilding. When a condensing appliance replaces an atmospheric one, the existing masonry chimney or B-vent is oversized and now unlined for wet flue gas. Flexible polypropylene liner in 25' and 35' kits drops down the existing chase and terminates at the top, which turns a chimney demolition into an afternoon.

Condensate has to have somewhere to go. Vent runs are sloped back toward the appliance so what forms in the pipe drains to the appliance's own trap, or into a drain tee and siphon where the geometry will not allow it. A vent that traps condensate in a low spot will eventually block, and the appliance will lock out on pressure rather than tell you why.

Venting sits alongside boilers and furnaces, tankless water heaters, condensate pumps and heating and HVAC.
